newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China sparks quarrel over HK residency rights.
newsitem.headline: China sparks quarrel over HK residency rights.

text.p: A move by Beijing to set the rules on who is entitled to permanent residency in Hong Kong after it reverts to China stirred up a quarrel in the British territory on Tuesday.
Beijing on Monday announced regulations on who would qualify for "right of abode" or permanent residency in Hong Kong after Britain hands back the territory on July 1.
Britain immediately accused China of going it alone on an issue that should have been settled in diplomatic negotiations.

Annoying Britain further, China has said it will submit the bill to a China-appointed provisional legislature, which will replace the elected Legislative Council on July 1, rather than to the current lawmaking body.
"It's our domestic affair. We don't need the British to tell us who is a Chinese national," reports from Beijing quoted China's top Hong Kong policy official, Lu Ping, as saying.
Contradicting Britain, Lu said the issue had never been on the agenda of Sino-British negotiations on the details of the sovereignty transfer.
Legislator James To of the Hong Kong Democratic Party accused China on Tuesday of "playing politics" by insisting the interim assembly should handle the bill on residency rights.
Pro-China politician Howard Young urged politicians to paper over their differences, so the law could be in place by July 1.

"I think whatever the situation, whatever the arguments, the most important thing is to take a pragmatic, down-to-earth attitude and get the laws passed as soon as possible for the benefit of those who would be affected," Young told local radio.
Hong Kong newspaper editorials were dominated by the controversy, which came only days after the community was rocked by another quarrel over China's plans to curb civil rights.

"China wants to play up the role of the provisional legislature to give it an important job so as to raise its image in the eyes of the Hong Kong people," the independent Hong Kong Economic Journal said.
The 60-member provisional legislature faces fierce opposition from the pro-democracy camp. Democrats have vowed to sue the body if it tries to make laws before July 1.

The South China Morning Post said both governments were ignoring the interests of Hong Kong people. "All too typically, what should be a perfectly simple arrangement is spoiled by bad feeling and in-fighting between the two governments involved."

The mass-selling Apple Daily said it had conducted a telephone survey showing that 51 percent of 470 polled wanted the current legislature to handle the issue, and not the China- controlled interim legislature. Only 19.8 percent believed it should be the task of the interim assembly.
The residency issue is close to the hearts of 750,000 Hong Kong people who possess foreign citizenship but who also cherish their permanent residency rights in Hong Kong.

Uncertainty has prompted a scramble for air tickets among migrants anxious to land in Hong Kong before midnight June 30, driven by prior suggestions by China that they would have to be in Hong Kong on July 1 or risk losing their right of abode.
China's latest pronouncement said Hong Kong emigrants could establish permanent right of abode in Hong Kong if they returned within 18 months of the handover.
Hong Kong Chinese could keep permanent residency status so long as they did not stay away for more than 36 months before resettling in the territory, it said.
